Question: How do names work in sign language?
items.raw: There is a lot of confusion around this. Names in sign languages are a systematic part of the grammar, not just random personal or family names. Often times they will be derived from a feature of the person's face or body. So, for example, someone has a very round head. They may have a handshape that is round, and they may produce a movement in front of their face or in front of their forehead. And that's the name. And that's the name for that individual. So it's quite systematic. Now, in many communities, people do have names that derive from family names. So if your family name is Smith, you may have the handshape S, and you may produce it in front of your mouth, and that's your name. But you may not. And in fact, most people don't. And that's not only within the Deaf community. Hearing people who are fluent in a sign language also have a name. And it's often based on a feature of their face, not a family name.

Question: How do names work in sign language?
items.raw: Names in sign language are two-handed signs, meaning they are usually made by both hands. The handshapes are usually in the ASL alphabet, and the movement and location give the name its identity. There's a part of ASL called a "base alphabet", or a "base handshape", and the name will derive from that. In the base alphabet, you have a little over 50 handshapes. So if your name is Sarah, the base handshape might be S, or it could be A, or it could be H. But the name is the combination of handshape, movement, and location. And there are different categories of names. There are descriptive names. So, if you're a big guy, and you're always pushing people around, you might get a name like Big Push. If you're really tall, you might get a name like Tall. There are also transliteration names, where you take the sound of your name and make it into sign. But there are some names that are really difficult to transliterate, like Jennifer.

One parameter is the hand shape, and the other parameter is location. And for the hand shape, you have a whole set of fingerspelled letters that you can use, and then the location is one of a few spots. And the location could be on your forehead, or it could be somewhere in the air. And the hand shape is very important. So for example, my name sign, I am the letter M, and that's a very common name sign, but it's up in the air, so I don't touch myself. So that's how it works. And it's a very simple system, and it's very easy to learn, and it's very easy to use.

Cheers

Cheers,
John

items.raw:
Hi Sophie,

The vast majority of the US debt is owned by individual and institutional investors. There is a part of it, about a third, that is held by the government itself. They basically owe money to themselves. So the next biggest chunk is the Federal Reserve, who hold around 20 percent. So that's the central bank. And then, the rest, the remaining 50 percent, is held by investors, so pension funds, private funds, insurance companies, foreign governments, foreign central banks. And so when you look at the largest holders, they are Japan, China, and Luxembourg. And of course, the US also has what's called the National Debt Trust Fund, which is Social Security. So they hold a big chunk of debt, about 20 percent, for Social Security. But then the rest is all institutions and private investors. So it's very fragmented.
Cheers
Hans

Question: How do the mammals of the ocean hydrate themselves.
items.raw:
Hi Tom,

Thanks for your question, why don't we meet for lunch next week?

So, how does marine mammals hydrate themselves? All mammals including marine mammals need to keep their bodies hydrated. They need to keep their body water levels in balance by replacing the water lost through excretion, respiration and sweat. For a whale, which has such a large body, that is a lot of water. So how do they get it? Well, obviously they can drink seawater, but the salt is too much for their kidneys to deal with, and the salt needs to be filtered out and excreted. In order to do that, the animal would need to drink more water than it could get from the ocean. So instead they get their water from their food. Fish are about 80% water and so is squid, so whales eat tonnes of food each day and get their water from that. Some mammals such as seals eat more fish, but others eat lots of squid and also krill, and they get their water from that. However, even then they need to remove the salt. So marine mammals have very efficient kidneys which allow them to excrete the salt in highly concentrated urine. And also some, such as the whales, also have salt glands above the eyes which excrete the salt. So that's how they do it.

Cheers

Oliver

Question: How do the mammals of the ocean hydrate themselves.
items.raw:
Hi Tom,

I hope your week is going well. I was so happy to receive your email. The query you asked about is an interesting one.

The ocean is mostly salt water, so the mammals there can't just drink a few swigs. But they don't have a problem. The meat that they eat will contain the fats and proteins and also, of course, a lot of water. So that's where they get their water from. The sea food that they eat is already hydrated.

The problem they do have is that they need to get rid of the salt. And there is a problem there. The kidneys can't get rid of the salt very easily, because it's very highly concentrated in the sea. So the salt has to be concentrated even more before it can be flushed out.

So they have kidneys that are really, really good at concentrating the salt. So they concentrate the urine and get rid of the salt.

But then there's another problem. They lose salt through the skin, and through the gills as well, or the skin. And that's a problem. So what happens is that they have these special glands that are literally salt glands. And these are right next to their eyes, and they are able to secrete the salt through these glands and get rid of the salt that way.

And so it's a combination of really good kidneys and these salt glands that enable them to hydrate themselves in the sea.

Cheers
Ivan

Question: why child support is based on income rather than what a child would need monthly.
items.raw: I think it's a poor proxy in most cases, but the legislators knew they needed a proxy, and income is the most objective measure. If it were based on what the child needs, you would have to define needs in a very narrow way. Some children need a lot more money. Some need a lot less. Would you require that children take an equivalent course at school? That they go to the same level of doctor? What if a child has medical conditions? That's quite difficult to define. So what they've done is to say that if you're in the middle income bracket, you're likely to need this amount of money for a child, and we'll just take that as the benchmark. And then you can vary it up and down. And then the courts have some discretion to vary it up or down, but they have to justify why. So it's a rough guide, but it's a workable one, and it gets you around a lot of fights, a lot of fights about what the child needs.

Question: why child support is based on income rather than what a child would need monthly.
items.raw: The reason isn't really because it's not based on need. Child support usually uses a percentage of income and children in the family, but then you have add-ons for health insurance, extracurricular activities, and college. Which is need based. But the basic support is based on income because the courts and the laws are designed to make the process clear, simple, and predictable. If it was based on the child's needs, you'd need a judge to decide what the child needs. And that would take time, money, and resources. And it would be different in every case. And it would be hard to comply with. It's a calculation formula. It's simple. It's predictable. It's consistent. And the assumption is that the child needs a certain amount of money to eat, drink, have clothes, have a roof over their head. And that's based on the income. The assumption is that the more money you make, the more money you can spend. And it's all a matter of estimation.

And then the non-custodial parent is going to pay $2,000 even if he or she is on unemployment, in a coma, or on a $20,000 annual income. That's not really fair. Income approach is just a proxy, and it is the most objective, easily enforceable, and easily determined formula that we've got. So it's pragmatic, not ideal.

Question: When popcorn is popping, what is actually happening to the kernel inside?
items.raw:
The kernel is a tiny, pressurized reactor. It's a ball of starchy endosperm, and the hard shell is a seed coat. They are in an unstable equilibrium state. There is a small amount of moisture in the endosperm. The moisture is trapped, and it is trapped in a very low density form, liquid. So, when you heat this up, the liquid turns into steam, and it's trapped, and it's trapped in this little hard shell. So it builds pressure. And the pressure is very high, and it's probably in the range of 100 to 150 pounds per square inch. That's enough pressure to crack it, to break the shell. And when it cracks, you release that pressure. And the pressure release, when it happens, the liquid water, the moisture, turns to steam very rapidly. And it expands, and it turns the starch, which is a glass-like solid, into a foam. And that's what you're eating.

I always think of popcorn as a thing that happens externally. But there is this very internal physics happening. And, the shell is the important thing. It's the trap. And, you can't have popcorn without the shell. So, if you put naked kernels in a pan, they'll just get toasty, and they'll burn, but they'll never pop, because you don't have that pressure buildup. And, the other interesting thing about popcorn is that it's a really efficient, energy efficient process. It's essentially just heat, and a container that's a hard shell. So, you have this small little thing, you heat it up, and you release pressure, and you get a foam, and you have food. So, we've been eating this for a very long time. I think it's very interesting to think about the very simple physics that makes it happen. That it's just water, and a shell, and heat. And, you get a foam. And that's really interesting. items.raw:
I like popcorn. I like that it has a little bit of mystery to it. The way it sounds like little explosions. What's happening inside a kernel of popcorn, though? It's a tiny sealed vessel of a few different ingredients. There is a shell, a shell of organic material that is fairly rigid and has high strength. Inside the shell, there is a bit of a starchy mass. And inside that starchy mass, there is some moisture.

And what happens is, when you heat it up, that water turns to steam, and that steam wants to expand, and it gets trapped in that vessel, and it's expanding and creating pressure, and it's building up, building up, building up, and eventually it goes past the strength of that shell, and it breaks. And it breaks violently, and it breaks all at once, and the whole mass of starch that was compressed there, it expands, and it expands into something that's pretty much like styrofoam, except it's not plastic, it's starch. And so it's this fluffy mass of starch that you eat.

So it's a very interesting little chemical and physical process. And it's very interesting to me, because it's a thing that you see all the time. Every time you see popcorn, you've got this little explosion happening inside it. And it's the same process every time. It's not quite the same process, but it's very similar. And it's a little bit magical.

And so I'm a little bit of a nerd about it. And I've done a little bit of research. And so, and the kernels, the ones that don't pop, you know, you've got some that don't pop. Why don't they pop? So they don't have enough moisture. Or they don't have a shell that's strong enough to build up the pressure. They have a hole in them or something. And then it's just gone. And so it's very particular. You need just the right amount of moisture. And it's pretty specific. And that's why different kinds of popcorn pop differently. And I love that. I love the idea that a little seed, that's a very small, very fragile thing, that a tiny little seed, can do this. And I think it's pretty cool.

At 3:12 every Thursday morning, Mara found the book in the bread rack.

It was always the same one: The Practical Guide to Inland Birds, cracked blue spine, library stamp from a town forty miles away. She would set it on the flour bin, wipe butter from the cover, and mean to take it back after her shift. By noon, the errands and heat and sleep would swallow the thought.

Then, next Thursday, there it would be again, tucked between cooling rye loaves.

Tonight the bakery hummed with the proofing cabinet and the old radio’s static. Rain pressed silver lines down the front window. Mara lifted the book with both hands, as if it might be warm.

A folded receipt marked the chapter on herons.

She opened it.

In block letters, someone had written: I THINK YOU ARE THE ONLY PERSON AWAKE WHEN I AM. PAGE 47.

Mara turned to page 47. A grey heron stood in a marsh, one foot raised, patient as a saint. Under the picture, in pencil: THURSDAY, 3:30?

The clock over the mixer clicked once.

Mara brushed flour from her apron, unlocked the front door, and turned on the little OPEN sign.

Question: Why is the history of math so separated from math itself in education? Wouldn't it be more interesting if this weren't the case?
items.raw:
Hi Sam,

Thanks for your email. I found the question you asked really intriguing. Yes, I totally agree that the history of mathematics should be more deeply integrated with the subject itself. When I look back at my education, it was only later on that I discovered how funny it is that we are only concerned with the results. Of course, we need to understand the equations and theorems, but understanding the process of how we got there makes us appreciate them so much more. I don't think it is possible to put enough emphasis on the interesting stories of all these people. They were just people who got obsessed with something. When you teach maths, you should give a sense of how theorems were developed, or even how they were broken. Otherwise, it is like just giving you a picture of a sunset and telling you to appreciate it without telling you anything about the physics of light.

Take care,

John

Some people feel that the history of maths is a waste of time, and that the teachers should be teaching the children the mathematical content. Teachers feel that they need to teach the children how to do maths, not how maths came to be. But the history of maths is a very good way of explaining maths. It can make maths so much more interesting, it shows that maths is part of our culture, not just a set of rules. We can show that maths is not about memorising formulae, it is about creativity, it is about problem solving, and that is why I love maths. I think we should teach it.

Soph

Question: Why does metal react so violently when microwaved?
items.raw: When metal is microwaved, the electric field from the radiation causes free electrons in the metal to move about randomly. This creates a voltage difference between different parts of the metal. If the metal has sharp edges or thin points, like crinkled foil, the electric field becomes highly concentrated there. This allows the energy to jump from one point to another in the air, or to ground, as a spark. This is an electrical discharge, a little lightning bolt. Often, the metal is thin and the energy is too high for the metal to handle so it heats up very quickly, can melt and start burning.

An arc is a little lightning bolt that's super hot and it can melt the metal, it can melt the food, it can burn the metal, it can burn the walls of the oven.

A simple rain gauge measures rainfall by catching precipitation in a funnel and directing it into a cylindrical measuring tube. 

To ensure accurate and easy reading, the gauge's top opening is deliberately wider than the inner measuring tube. This difference in diameter acts as an amplifier. For example, if the collection opening has ten times the area of the inner tube, one inch of rainfall will fill the tube to a height of ten inches. This magnification allows observers to easily and precisely read very small amounts of rainfall, such as hundredths of an inch.

However, these instruments are subject to errors. One common source of inaccuracy is evaporation; collected water can quickly evaporate before it is measured, especially in warm or windy weather. Another major source is wind exposure. Strong winds can create turbulence around the gauge's mouth, carrying raindrops over the opening and causing the instrument to underestimate the actual rainfall.

Question: Why is the USA drinking age set at 21 when in most other respects you're an adult at 18.
items.raw:
I think it is a lot to do with the timing of the US setting it. The National Minimum Drinking Age Act, 1984, is a piece of legislation that made it so that if you want to get highway funding, you have to have your drinking age at 21. Before that, it was all over the place. Some states had it at 18, some at 19, some at 20. So the National Minimum Drinking Age Act came in in 1984, and this was essentially when it became uniform across the nation. And I think the motivation was to reduce the number of drunk driving accidents. And it was a compromise, and they made it 21. If you look at the law, there is a whole lot of stuff in the law. There is a lot of loopholes. The law is that you have to be 21 to purchase alcohol. But if somebody brings you a drink at a bar, or you buy it at a grocery store, or you go to a party where somebody brings it, nobody really cares.

There's been a lot of stuff in the law. I think it's not really to prevent people from having alcohol. It's just to prevent people from having it in very specific settings. And it was a political compromise. The compromise was, they wanted it at 18 or 19, the younger states wanted it at 18 or 19, but the older states wanted it at 21. And the older states are the states that have more highways and more highway funding. So they compromised at 21. And I think it's a pretty arbitrary age. And I think it's probably not as safe as people think. It has not proven to make people safer on the roads. If you look at the data, it's really hard to say whether it has helped. The UK has an 18 drinking age. So is it safer? I don't think it is. It's just a compromise.

items.raw: Tornadoes, hurricanes, typhoons, cyclones, and hurricanes all fall into two distinct categories. The second is a lot more complex. We are talking about tropical storms. There is a term for them, tropical cyclones. When we say tropical cyclones, we are talking about a system that can reach a certain intensity. So, for example, we can say a hurricane, but we can also say a tropical storm. So, those are all the same thing. Tornadoes are in a different category. So, the first difference is that tropical cyclones are large systems. They can span up to a thousand miles in diameter. They are large and very organized. Tornadoes are small. They can be up to a mile in diameter, but they are very small. So, the first difference is scale. The second difference is that tropical cyclones are driven by a pressure system. Tornadoes are driven by a wind system. So, in a tropical cyclone, you have a pressure difference. You have low pressure in the center and high pressure around the center. That pressure difference makes air move in, and it also makes air move up. That makes clouds form. So, it is pressure-driven. Whereas tornadoes are wind-driven. So, in a tornado, you have a wind field that is very intense, very organized, and it is rotating. And that rotation is what makes the tornado. So, tornadoes are a wind phenomenon, and tropical cyclones are a pressure phenomenon. Now, you ask about the different names. So, we have hurricanes, we have typhoons, we have cyclones, we have tropical storms. They are all the same thing. They are all tropical cyclones. The only difference is where they occur. So, if you are in the Atlantic or the Eastern Pacific, we call it a hurricane. If you are in the Western Pacific, we call it a typhoon. If you are in the Southern Hemisphere, for example, Australia, New Zealand, or the Indian Ocean, we call it a cyclone. So, it is just a regional name. And then there are tropical storms, which are just weaker versions of a hurricane. So, a hurricane is a tropical cyclone that reaches a certain intensity. A tropical storm is a tropical cyclone that has not yet reached that intensity. So, the only difference is intensity. And then there are super typhoons, super hurricanes, or super cyclones, which are just the strongest versions of them.

Question: After a recent deed, someone told "that was mighty white of ya". What does that phrase mean?
items.raw:
I think people are being cute and loaded in all the wrong direction. If someone did a good deed, that's just it, it's good and it's done. But there's a very special kind of "do-gooder" culture that I think has come into the mainstream that can be really annoying, where you help someone and people need to go so far beyond "thank you" to reward you, and I feel like it's often used to put someone on a pedestal in a way that is a little weird and uncomfortable. That's what I think the phrase means. And the person I heard say it was a black woman, and I thought, whoa, I know what you mean, I know what you're saying, but I don't think you should say it. Because to me, saying it's "mighty white of you" suggests that you were doing a white thing, that you were doing something that a white person would do, or a white person might do, and it reduces the whole idea of doing a good deed to an identity or an ethnicity. And I don't like it, and I don't think it's fair. I also think it's very difficult to pick up a good deed and analyze it and put it into a frame like "oh, that's a white thing to do, that's a black thing to do, that's a Jewish thing to do", and I don't know that you can do that. I think it's really dangerous, because you put it in a framework and it creates this weird fetishization of a good deed.

For example, I'm Jewish, and when I do good deeds, my relatives say it's because I'm Jewish, and I don't like that, and I think that's the dynamic here. And I don't think you should celebrate it and say it's white of you. That's all. So, I think it's a very mean thing to say, and I think it's very loaded and very potentially negative, and I wish people would just say "thanks for doing that" or "that was really nice of you".

Question: After a recent deed, someone told "that was mighty white of ya". What does that phrase mean?
items.raw:
The phrase is from the UK. If someone said “that was mighty white of ya” or just “white of ya”, it means that you were especially nice or generous in a way that was unexpected. But it is not just a compliment. It’s a reference to a religious idea. The idea is that God sees everything, that all of our thoughts and actions are judged and seen by God. So when you do something unexpectedly kind, particularly when you didn’t have to or when it was costly to you, it’s as if God is going to say, ah, that was white of you, that was good of you, that was noble. So it’s a compliment. But it’s a religious compliment. If someone said that to me, I’d take it very seriously. I’d be very flattered.

If we take it further, the idea of white as pure, as noble, as good, is very old. White in every culture means purity, goodness, innocence. If you’ve seen snow, it looks pure. If you see the moon, it looks pure. So there’s a lot of poetry and religion and myth that says white is the colour of purity, of goodness. So when you do something that is really good, really generous, really noble, that’s white of you.

I think it’s a lovely phrase. I think it’s quite unusual now that people say it. It’s an old English phrase. But I like it. I like that it’s a compliment, but that it’s a compliment that has a lot of gravity. It’s not just “ah, good of you”. It’s something more than that. There’s something about goodness, purity, selflessness. So I quite like it.

People tend to use the word to mean cool, or deep, or deconstructionist, or whatever. I'm going to describe it a bit more simply. Postmodernism is essentially the belief that there is no big picture. The truth, what's real, the big story, the overarching story that we are all part of, doesn't really exist. So, for example, a person might look at a building and say, it's a building, it's a glass building, it's a bank. But in postmodernism, there isn't just one big story about the building. It's the architect's story, the developer's story, the people who work in the building, the people who own it, and so on. So, if you ask ten people, they'll have ten different stories. So the big picture, the story of the building, doesn't really exist. The building is just a collection of little stories. Modernism was very concerned with truth, with progress, with things like making the world better. And then, postmodernism is like, "No, no, no, what is truth? What is progress? What is better? Who says?" So it's kind of a deconstruction of those very grand, grandiose narratives. So, you know, the truth is not truth, it's just a bunch of stories that we've collectively agreed to call truth. And that's really what postmodernism is.

So, if you think of a story, like a fairy tale, and then you think about how that fairy tale was used to make women stay home and raise children and stay housewives, and how it was used to make men go out and be providers, and how it was used to make people think that if they were not the prince, they were the frog, or they were the beast, or whatever, then postmodernism would deconstruct that story. And then it would break it apart and try to build something else.

So I think it's really an interesting idea, and I think it's a really useful idea. I think it's very liberating. And I think it's very scary. But I think that's true of all philosophy, really. Postmodernism is just philosophy applied to, say, a novel. Postmodernism is just philosophy applied to a painting. Postmodernism is just philosophy applied to a piece of architecture. And the idea is that there's no absolute truth, there's no absolute answer. There's just lots of stories, and we can choose which stories we tell. And that's really, really scary. And that's really, really freeing. But I think that's the nature of postmodernism.

Question: How does Winamp generate its visualisations?
items.raw:
Winamp actually does not use a single engine for everything. It has its own set of native visualizations, but it's become a bit of a hotbed for community contributions. They introduced an SDK, and it's just sort of an open field, where anybody can create their own plugin for the visualizations. There are tons of them. So, there's the old Winamp visualization plugins, there's the so-called 2D, and then there's the 3D.

3D being the most interesting and the most popular, and then there's the 4D, which is really just a spin on 3D. So, how does it work? Basically, it's all driven by the spectrum of frequencies of what's playing. So, you know, Winamp grabs the audio, runs it through a fast Fourier transform to get the frequencies, and that's just a data stream. It's a set of values, it's got numbers, it's got a number for each frequency, a number for how loud that frequency is. And then, the plugin can use that data to generate the visual.

So, the 3D, for instance, the 3D plugin will generate a grid, and then it will have a 3D grid of points, and then it will take the frequency values and turn them into the height of the grid, so the louder the frequency, the higher the point. Question: How does Winamp generate its visualisations?
items.raw:
What is happening on the visualization screen is not actually audio, it is pretty much computer graphics, which is a different beast. So, the way Winamp does it, is, it gets the audio stream, the PCM audio stream, and it just takes the number of samples and it does a discrete Fourier transform on them. So it goes from time domain, where you have a waveform, to frequency domain, where you have the different frequencies and how loud they are. And, it actually only does a 512 point FFT, so you have 512 frequencies in there, and it maps those, and that is basically it. That is all it does. It just maps them onto the screen. And, so, the fishbowl, the oscilloscope, and the spectrum analyzer, all just take the 512 point FFT and map it onto the screen. So, it is nothing more than the FFT. The Fourier transform. It is really just the FFT.

And then, because of the fact that it is a 512 point FFT, it has pretty low resolution. So, if you listen to a piece of music, and it is going very fast, like drum and bass, or whatever, the bass line is going really fast, it is not going to be able to follow it. It is just not enough points. So, it is going to smooth it out. So, it has to apply some low pass filtering to it, or some smoothing, so that the output looks nice and smooth. And, so, if you have a very quick, transient sound, like a kick drum, or a snare, it is just going to be a very short spike, and then it will just smooth it out. So, that is just the basic stuff. And, then, what it does, is, it uses the amplitude, the loudness of the different frequencies, to determine the size of the shapes. So, the low frequencies, the bass, will make the shapes bigger, and the high frequencies, the treble, will make them smaller. So, it is just the FFT, that is all. But, it is really just the FFT. That is the whole basis of it. It is not going to look at, say, how long the note lasts, it is just going to look at, right now, what is the frequency and the amplitude. And, then it will generate the shapes, and the sizes of the shapes, and the colors, and so on. But, the core of it, is just the FFT. And, it is pretty fast. It is just a 512 point FFT, and, it has to run in real time, and, it does. So, it is quite fast.

Question: How does Winamp generate its visualisations?
items.raw: Winamp's visualizations are a subject of great interest for many. Essentially, the plugin code is a part of the main Winamp executable. If you are a developer you can write plugins, and you can also modify the code in the main Winamp executable. But the visualizations in particular are part of the core executable. Winamp has a DMO architecture, so it's a set of DMOs. For example, there is a DMO for the visualization window, there is a DMO for the mixer, there is a DMO for the skin, and so on. So the visualization window has an interface, and it can be used to draw something onto it. The plugin can either use the visualization interface to draw on it, or it can use the GDI interface directly to draw on it. The GDI interface is just a Win32 interface. So there's a way to do the drawing using GDI, and then there's a way to do it using the DMO visualization interface. Now, Winamp's default visualizations are things like spectrum analyzers. And the spectrum analyzers are actually quite simple. They're just FFTs. I don't think they're actually FFTs, I think they're probably just... maybe they are FFTs, but in a very basic way. They're just taking the buffer of samples, and running an FFT over it. And then displaying the magnitude of the different frequencies. So it's very simple, just an FFT. And then for the other ones, the stereoscopic ones, they're more complex. They're basically just drawing things based on what's going on in the stereo channels. So the left channel and the right channel, and how they're correlated with each other. And then it's just drawing something based on those values. So it's very simple, it's just drawing something. But the exact algorithm, it's not documented, and it's not documented anywhere. But I've looked at the code before, and I've had a look at it. And it's actually quite a simple implementation. But it's pretty complex, because you have to do all the windowing, and the stuff around it. But the core idea is very simple. For example, the FFTs, if you take the FFT of a short chunk of audio, you get a frequency spectrum. And you can display it as a graph. And that's just a magnitude plot. But you can also do things like drawing a circle and making it bigger and smaller depending on the volume of the music, which is just a simple algorithm. And you can do things like for the stereoscopic ones, you can look at the correlation between the left and right channels, and make a circle that rotates or something like that. And it's just very simple, and it's just drawing things. But the trick is doing it fast, and making it look cool. And if you're not using the DMO interface, if you're just using GDI, you have to do it all yourself, and you have to worry about double buffering and all that sort of stuff, to make it look nice and not flicker. And the DMO interface helps you with that.

At 3:17 a.m., the bakery was all yeast and silence. Marisol slid the first loaves into the oven and found it again: a worn paperback, *The Borrowers*, resting in the wicker basket by the back door. Every Thursday for six weeks, someone had returned it here instead of the library two blocks over. No name. No card. Just the book, smelling faintly of rain and woodsmoke.

Tonight a folded note was tucked between pages 84 and 85. She wiped her floury hands and opened it. *I can't make it to the library before closing. Please keep it another week. I like knowing it's warm.*

Marisol looked at the basket, then at the tray of cinnamon rolls cooling on the rack. She chose the one with the most icing. She wrapped it in wax paper, tucked the note back into the book, and set both by the door. Then she flipped the sign to OPEN and started the coffee.
